## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ghatāsanajātaka* (Ja 133), rendered in English as *Like a Fire Consuming Ghee*, is a narrative belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon. In the canonical commentary edited by V. Fausböll, the verse opens with the incipit *Khemam yahin ti* [Fausböll 1877]. The framing narrative is set while the Buddha was residing at Jetavana and concerns a monk who, after receiving a meditation topic (*kammaṭṭhāna*) from the Master, took up residence in a forest dwelling near a hamlet where his leaf hut burned down during his almsround [Fausböll 1877].

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta appears as a leader or king of birds (*sakuṇarājā*) [Fausböll 1877]. When peril arose, the birds who obeyed the Bodhisatta's advice flew away to safety, whereas those who failed to heed his words were destroyed [Fausböll 1877]. Concluding the discourse with the truths (*saccāni*), the Buddha reveals the connection between the past and present lives (*samodhāna*): the obedient birds were his present followers (*buddhaparisā*), and the king of birds was the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1877].
